title: URL Shortener
summary: Turn long links into short ones and redirect fast, at scale.
problem: Design a service that creates short links for long URLs and redirects visitors who open them. Think of bit.ly.
functional: Create a short link for a URL, optionally with a custom alias and an expiry
Redirect a short link to the long URL
nonFunctional: Redirects must be very fast (p99 under 50 ms) and highly available
Short codes must not be guessable in order, and never collide
constraints: 100 million new links a month, 10 billion redirects a month
Links are kept for 5 years by default
deliverables: Requirements and the assumptions you made
A capacity estimate (requests per second, storage, bandwidth)
A high-level architecture diagram (Mermaid or an uploaded image)
The API (endpoints and payloads) and the data model
How it scales, how it fails, and what you would monitor
The main trade-offs and what you chose not to build
hints: Estimate first: how many bytes per record, how many redirects per second?
How do you generate a unique short code without a single bottleneck?
reference:
### Sketch
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  U[Client] --> CDN[CDN / edge cache]
  CDN --> LB[Load balancer]
  LB --> API[Stateless API servers]
  API --> C[(Cache: code to URL)]
  API --> DB[(Key-value store: code, url, expiry)]
  API --> Q[[Click events queue]]
  Q --> A[Analytics workers] --> OLAP[(Counts store)]
```

### Numbers
Assumptions, not measurements. 100 M links a month is about 40 writes/s and 10 B redirects a month is about 4,000 redirects/s on average (30 days is about 2.6 M seconds), with peaks of, say, 10x. 100 M x 12 months x 5 years x ~500 B per record (an assumption) is about 3 TB: a key-value store partitioned by code is enough, and at 40 writes/s a single well-run relational database with a unique index on the code would also cope for a long time.

### Decisions
- **Code generation**: a counter handed out in ranges to each API server (no coordination per request), encoded in base62 and shuffled with a keyed permutation so codes are not sequential. 7 characters give 3.5 trillion codes.
- **Other ways to make a code**: hash the long URL and keep a prefix (the same URL gets the same code, but you must detect collisions and retry); a random code with a conditional insert that retries on conflict (no counter to run, at the price of occasional retries as the space fills); or a pool of pre-generated codes. The counter-range design is chosen here because it never collides and needs no retry; the others are simpler to operate.
- **Redirect path**: edge cache, then an in-memory cache, then the store. Use **302** (or 307) if you need every click counted at the server, **301** (or 308) if you accept browsers caching the redirect. A CDN that caches the redirect also hides those clicks from the origin, so either count at the edge or accept undercounting.
- **Availability**: the store is replicated; redirects work from replicas, creating a link needs the primary.
- **Analytics** is asynchronous through a queue, so a failing analytics system never slows a redirect.
- **Abuse**: rate limit creation, scan target URLs, allow takedown.
